beats.narration_text: Six terms. An estimator is a rule that turns data into a number. A base rate is how common an outcome is in a group. A label is the answer a model learns to predict. A proxy is a feature that stands in for something else. A protected group is a group shielded from unfair treatment. And a causal graph is a set of arrows showing what causes what.

beats.narration_text: In the newspapers, bias means unfair or prejudiced. That meaning is built for moral clarity, not for engineering. In statistics, bias is a property of an estimator, a rule that turns data into a number. The formal meaning gives up the moral punch and buys you something you can act on: it tells you where to intervene.

beats.narration_text: Call the true quantity theta, and your estimate theta hat. Bias is the expected value of theta hat, minus theta. Zero means unbiased: maybe wrong on any one dataset, but not systematically wrong. Nonzero means systematically off, in one direction.

beats.narration_text: Here's the consequence that matters most. More data will not fix a biased estimator. It converges, with growing confidence, to the wrong answer. More data narrows the scatter. It doesn't move the offset.

beats.narration_text: Peverill Squire's nineteen eighty-eight analysis found two problems working together. beats.narration_text: Here are the ten, as places in a pipeline where the estimate can drift from the truth. Selection and sampling, when people are collected. Data entry, when they're recorded. beats.narration_text: Start with selection bias, and watch how it enters. You write a reasonable query: patients with a complete lab panel within six hours of admission. Nobody decides to exclude anyone. The exclusion rides in on the reasonableness.

beats.narration_text: Your estimator computes the average outcome among the people in your sample. You wanted the average in the population. Those two are equal on exactly one condition: whether you land in the sample must not depend on the outcome. The moment it does, the estimate is biased before a single parameter is fit.

beats.narration_text: Take a sepsis model, as an illustration. The patients too critical to have labs drawn on time are exactly the ones who most need the alert, and the six-hour filter drops them. The model learns what predicts sepsis among the stable, then is asked about the unstable. It underestimates their risk.

beats.narration_text: You can correct for selection you observed. Inverse probability weighting gives each kept person a weight of one over their chance of being kept, so survivors stand in for the people dropped. In the same simulation, the naive estimate is about eighteen percent. Weighted, it's about thirty.

beats.narration_text: Five more mechanisms share a spine: somewhere a person exercises judgment, and their prior leaks into the record. Confirmation bias is a researcher's prior shaping what gets collected, kept and reported. Observer bias is that prior inside one measurement, like an annotator who knows the earlier diagnosis.

beats.narration_text: Self-report bias is the subject's own prior: people report voting more and drinking less than they do. Data-coding bias enters when judgment squeezes material into categories. beats.narration_text: None of these five entered through the model. They entered upstream of the data, when a human judged. So the fixes look like organizational practice: pre-registration, blinding, adversarial review. Engineers reach past them because they don't look like engineering, which is exactly why the bias survives.

beats.narration_text: Two more are quieter, and people mistake them for noise. Data-entry bias is patterned transcription error: a form that buries the accurate diagnosis code three menus deep gets the nearest code instead, and a whole class of conditions is undercoded in one direction. Verify against source documents; don't auto-correct.

beats.narration_text: Sampling bias is selection's accessibility cousin: some groups are under-represented because they were hard to reach, not because of their outcomes. beats.narration_text: Now the one that breaks the pattern. In every mechanism so far, something was wrong with the data: a filter, a prior, a slip. Historical bias has none of that. beats.narration_text: So the fixes can't be data-quality fixes; there's no defect to repair. They lower the leverage of the historical signal on today's prediction: a less-biased proxy for the outcome, a fairness constraint, or weighting recent records over records from more discriminatory periods. Each trades predictive fit for less inheritance, and a person decides how much fit to spend.

beats.narration_text: Implicit bias, the unconscious associations of the people in the pipeline, isn't really a tenth peer. It isn't an entry point. beats.narration_text: Because it has no single point, it resists a point fix. One handle is a downstream audit: compare the rate of positive predictions across groups. But read a gap as a flag, not a verdict, since real differences in base rates produce the same gap. The fixes with leverage are structural: diverse teams, structured decisions, continuous auditing.
